newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mulls state electricity-transaction fee.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mulls state electricity-transaction fee.

text.p: The Clinton administration may give states a green light to impose fees on the electricity industry to fund research, low-income energy assistance and other uses, Energy Secretary Federico Pena said Monday.
Pena told an electricity industry convention that the administration aimed to ensure investment in such areas as the industry was deregulating.
A number of measures to steer investment were being considered, he said.

"We're concerned about investments in technology and research and investment," Pena told the meeting of the Edison Electric Institute. "I don't think it's wise to rely exclusively on the market to sustain our nation's investment in these vital areas.

"One mechanism under consideration is providing states with a clear jurisidictional basis for imposing, if they so choose, fees on all electricity transactions to fund investments in energy efficiency, renewable energy technology, research and development and low-income assistance," he said.
Another option is a fund, proposed by some in Congress, similar to a universal-service fund authorized under telecommunications industry deregulation in 1996.
Such a fund, Pena said, would be supported by a "broad based, competitively neutral, and very small system-benefits charge," collected at a transmission or systems operation level.
Money raised through the funds would be matched with state support for programs on renewable energy, conservation, energy efficiency, research and development or universal service.

Also being considered was a system to encourage use of renewable energy sources by requring electricity sellers to hold "renewable energy credits" equivalent to a percentage of their total sales, Pena said.
"No final decisions have been made on any of these options," he said.
Pena said he expected the administration's proposed blueprint for electricity deregulation would be completed by early July.
Several states have already begun their own deregulation programs, and it remains unclear how influential the federal involvement will be.
Pena said in developing the proposals for a deregulated energy system, the Engergy Department was following five main principles.

The system should promote competition, ensure reliability and efficiency of service, respect the physical and institutional "complexities" of the current electricity system, maintain universal service and allow states flexibility to adopt structures best suited to their individual needs, he said.

He said a deregulated electricity industry could have environmental benefits, and noted that pilot programs had drawn an enthusiastic response at several companies allowing customers to choose -- and pay a premium for -- energy derived from environmentally friendly sources.
